system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, chronic pancreatitis, and asthma was admitted for worsening epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, and alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He had been drinking heavily and presented with tremors and hallucinations consistent with delirium tremens. His pain was attributed to an acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis, despite a normal lipase. He also had mild alcoholic hepatitis with elevated AST and bilirubin, and an asthma exacerbation requiring albuterol nebulizers and a steroid burst. He was managed with CIWA protocol for withdrawal, IV fluids, pain control with hydromorphone, and respiratory support. His condition improved over five days—he stabilized, tolerated a regular diet, and had resolution of withdrawal symptoms. He was discharged home with pain medication, continued liver and asthma therapies, and referrals for alcohol rehabilitation and follow-up care.

diagnoses.long_title: Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without ascites

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad stomach pain, mostly in the middle, going to my back. And I can’t catch my breath well. I’ve been feeling shaky and weird since I left detox last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you had seizures the night before coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, three of them. I was scared, so I started drinking that morning to calm down. But then the pain got worse and I couldn’t breathe right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your alcohol level was high when you arrived, and you were given diazepam in the ER to help prevent more seizures. We’re concerned about alcohol withdrawal, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to go through withdrawal again. Last time was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on a scheduled dose of diazepam to prevent that. We’re also giving you IV thiamine and folate—important because of your history with alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the stomach pain? Feels like it did last time I had pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase was slightly elevated, and given your history, we think this is another flare of pancreatitis. We’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No food? How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with IV fluids and pain meds. Once your pain improves and you’re not needing IV pain medicine as often, we’ll try advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already hungry. But the pain is bad—can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving you Dilaudid through the IV for now. It’s stronger and works faster. We’ll monitor your pain closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the breathing? I’ve been wheezing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a history of asthma, and your exam shows wheezing. Your chest X-ray showed a small opacity in the left lung, but it’s likely atelectasis or early inflammation. We’re treating it as an asthma flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been intubated before during asthma attacks. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re giving you albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers and a steroid burst—prednisone—for five days. That should help calm the airways and prevent things from getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my methadone? I take 50 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve confirmed your dose with the clinic and will continue it daily. It’s important to keep that consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also have this toothache—left upper molar. It’s been killing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam, I see decay in a few teeth. We can’t treat it here, but you should see a dentist after discharge. Chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition can worsen dental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound from this morning showed a large liver and an enlarged spleen, which fits with your cirrhosis. But the good news—the portal vein is open, so no blockage causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver’s still bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the cirrhosis is chronic, and your AST and bilirubin are elevated, suggesting some ongoing liver inflammation—mild alcoholic hepatitis. But no new damage we can see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg was swollen, so we did a Doppler ultrasound. No blood clot—good news. But the redness and swelling might be from poor circulation or skin irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for a while. It gets itchy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be intertrigo—skin inflammation in folds. We’ll recommend a cream and keeping the area dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low iron and hemoglobin. We think it’s from poor diet and possible slow GI bleeding, given your history of gastritis. We’re giving IV iron to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me feel more tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it should help with energy over time. Anemia can make you feel weak and short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I try eating something? I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try a small amount of clear liquid. But if the pain comes back, we may need to hold off and keep you on IV meds a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So you tried eating yesterday, but the pain got worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I thought I was ready, but it flared right back. I want the IV pain med back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll restart the IV Dilaudid and try again in a day or two. This is common with pancreatitis—it can take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making progress. Your breathing is better, you’re not wheezing as much, and your withdrawal symptoms have improved. We’ve stopped the CIWA protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain, continue the steroid for asthma, and slowly reintroduce food. Once you’re stable on oral pain meds and eating, we can talk about discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re doing well. You’re breathing comfortably, your pain is controlled with oral Dilaudid, and you’ve tolerated a low-fat diet. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I get pain meds to take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sending you home with opioids. But you should follow up with your PCP about your chronic pain. They can help decide if you need anything long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What else should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the prednisone—just one more dose today. Stay on a low-fat diet for a few weeks to protect your pancreas. And please follow up with your hepatologist and a dentist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep taking my acamprosate and methadone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Those are important for recovery. We’re also sending you home with your regular liver and asthma meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try to stay sober this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the most important thing. Your body’s been through a lot. Staying off alcohol will help everything—your liver, pancreas, and overall health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Take care, and call your doctor if anything worsens.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, chronic pancreatitis, and asthma was admitted for severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, shortness of breath, and recent seizures following alcohol detox. He had been drinking heavily to manage withdrawal symptoms, which triggered an acute flare of pancreatitis and an asthma exacerbation. He was managed with IV fluids, pain control using IV then oral Dilaudid, benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal prophylaxis, and a steroid burst for asthma. His symptoms improved over three days—he stabilized neurologically, tolerated a low-fat diet, and had resolution of respiratory distress. He received IV iron for iron deficiency anemia and was discharged home with instructions to continue his medications, complete the prednisone course, maintain a low-fat diet, and follow up with his PCP, hepatologist, and dentist.
